eras.note: Joseph Bonaparte's reign is dated from June or August 1808 depending on the source, to 11 December 1813; the Peninsular War ended on 17 April 1814. An 1810 Napoleonic division of Spain into 84 prefectures is recorded.
Navarre is listed as a province in the 1833 division, and the Convention of Bergara of 1839 led to a reduced form of home rule.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — province under the Ley Paccionada
eras.note: The Ley Paccionada of 1841 made Navarre a province and moved the customs to the Pyrenees.

Civil registration is dated from 1871 (FamilySearch's church-records page says 1869), with some municipalities holding records from as early as 1837; the records are still in each municipality's archive, and certificates are requested through the Ministerio de Justicia. During the Third Carlist War, 1872-1876, a Basque state with Estella as its capital existed until Alfonso XII's restoration; the Gamazada rising of 1893-1894 in Pamplona opposed Madrid's breaches of the 1841 provisions.
The Second Republic dates from 1931; the Nationalist military uprising began in Pamplona on 18 July 1936.

eras.polity: Nationalist zone, Franco's State, then the transition to the 1978 Constitution
eras.note: The Nationalists took over Navarre in July 1936; in 1937 Navarre kept its own economic arrangement while the agreement was abolished for Biscay and Gipuzkoa. In 1955 Viana and Amescoas passed from the diocese of Calahorra to Pamplona.
The Chartered Community of Navarre is dated 1982, with its Statute of Autonomy of 16 August 1982.

regions.label: Catalonia
regions.sub: Barcelona, Girona, Manresa, Vilafranca del Penedès, Tremp, Cervera, Montblanc, Igualada, Vilanova i la Geltrú

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Principality of Catalonia (own Constitutions, Generalitat and Courts)
eras.note: Parish registers follow the Council of Trent (1545 and 1563). Most registers older than 100 years have moved to the diocesan archive of the parish's diocese, for example the Arxiu Històric Arxidiocesà de Tarragona, which received a parish baptism book begun in 1563 in 2025. The Generalitat, General Court and Consell de Cent were abolished at the end of this era.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Nueva Planta (Captain General replaces viceroy)
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Catalan Nueva Planta decree is dated 9 October 1715 (issued) or 16 January 1716 (dispatched), depending on the source. It replaced Catalan with Spanish as the administrative language of the Royal Audience and closed the six Catalan universities in favour of a royal university at Cervera.

eras.polity: French Empire — departments of Montserrat (Barcelona), Ter (Girona), Sègre and Bouches-de-l'Èbre (Lleida)
eras.note: Annexed by a French decree of 26 January 1812 that was never published in the Bulletin des Lois and never officially validated even by France. The four departments were merged into two on 7 March 1813 and suppressed on 10 March 1814. Whether civil registers were kept in them is not established here.
Parish registers are the record until civil registration in 1871.

Civil registration begins in 1871 under the law of 17 June 1870, though some municipalities have records from as early as 1837. The registers stay in each municipality's local archive; certified copies come from the Ministerio de Justicia or the local Juzgado de Paz / Oficina del Registro Civil.

eras.polity: Second Spanish Republic — Catalonia autonomous from 1932
eras.note: The Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931; Catalonia had home rule from 1932, with a parliament and president of its own. Nationalist forces occupied Barcelona on 26 January 1939, Girona on 2 February, and reached the French frontier on 9-10 February. The Civil War destroyed or scattered parish records: in one Tarragona-diocese parish, sacramental books went missing after July 1936 and the oldest was returned to the archive only in 2025.
Under Franco's State, Catalan autonomy was abolished and the Catalan language and Catalan Christian names were banned.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Catalonia an autonomous community
eras.note: A Statute of Autonomy was approved by referendum in 1979 and a new one took effect on 9 August 2006. The Arxiu Nacional de Catalunya (Sant Cugat del Vallès, created by decree on 28 November 1980) holds government and private fonds, not the parish registers, which are in the diocesan archives.

regions.label: The Valencian country
regions.sub: Valencia, Alzira, Dénia, Castelló, Alicante

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Kingdom of Valencia (own Furs)
eras.note: James I took the city of Valencia on 9 October 1238. Parish registers follow the Council of Trent (1545 and 1563). The Moriscos were expelled in 1609, roughly 125,000 people. The Furs ended in 1707.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Nueva Planta (Castilian law)
eras.note: After the Battle of Almansa (25 April 1707) the Furs of Valencia were repealed by the decree of 29 June 1707, and Valencia was governed by Castilian law. Castilian became the language of government and the courts.

eras.polity: French occupation — Valencia under Marshal Suchet
eras.note: Marshal Suchet forced the city to surrender on 8 January 1812; in mid-1812 Joseph Bonaparte moved his court to Valencia; the French left in July 1813.

Before 1833 the area was divided into four provinces (Alicante, Castellón, Valencia and Xàtiva); from 1833 the current three-province system was consolidated, so older papers may sit under a province that no longer exists. Parish registers are the record until civil registration in 1871.

Civil registration begins in 1871 under the law of 17 June 1870, though some municipalities have records from as early as 1837. The registers stay in each municipality's local archive; certified copies come from the Ministerio de Justicia or the local Juzgado de Paz / Oficina del Registro Civil.

eras.polity: Second Spanish Republic — Valencia the Republican capital 1936-37
eras.note: Valencia became the capital of Republican Spain on 6 November 1936 and the government moved to Barcelona on 31 October 1937. The city surrendered on 30 March 1939. The first attempt at Valencian self-government was suspended by the war.
Under Franco's State.
The Statute of Autonomy dates from 1982 (a second in 2006). Valencian and Spanish are both official languages; Valencian is the local name for the language also known as Catalan.

regions.label: Mallorca
regions.sub: Palma, Inca, Llucmajor, Santa Margalida, s'Arenal

eras.polity: James I's conquest — the Kingdom of Majorca (from 1276)
eras.note: Before registers. James I of Aragon took Palma at the end of 1229; the Kingdom of Majorca was created in 1276 and took in Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera, with Roussillon and Cerdanya. It passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1344 or 1349 depending on the source (Peter IV invaded in 1343; James III was killed at Llucmajor on 25 October 1349).

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Kingdom of Majorca (own viceroy)
eras.note: The kingdom remained separate, with its own viceroy and the same king as Aragon, until 1715. Parish registers follow the Council of Trent (1545 and 1563).

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Nueva Planta (Balearic province from 1833)
eras.note: The Nueva Planta decree for Mallorca is dated 28 November 1715; it partly repealed the Mallorcan franqueses and made Castilian the language of government. The Balearics became a Spanish province in 1833. Parish registers are the record until civil registration in 1871.

Civil registration begins in 1871 under the law of 17 June 1870, though some municipalities have records from as early as 1837. The registers stay in each municipality's local archive; certified copies come from the Ministerio de Justicia or the local Juzgado de Paz / Oficina del Registro Civil.
The Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931.
Mallorca supported the Nationalists; Republican forces failed to take it in the August 1936 Battle of Majorca. Under Franco's State.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Balearic Islands autonomous community
eras.note: The islands gained self-government under their first Statute of Autonomy in 1983.

regions.label: Menorca
regions.sub: Maó, Ciutadella, Es Castell, Sant Lluís

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — conquered by Alfonso III
eras.note: Before registers. Alfonso III of Aragon invaded on 17 January 1287; the island was briefly ceded to the Kingdom of Mallorca and the king of Aragon retook it in 1343. Sources conflict on the earlier date: Muslim rule until 1231, or a fall in 1232. Ciutadella was the capital until 1722.

eras.polity: Britain — captured by Anglo-Dutch forces in 1708, ceded at Utrecht in 1713
eras.note: THE TRAP. Menorca was not under Spain from 1708: Spain formally ceded it in 1713, the capital moved to Mahón in 1722 and the Royal Navy based itself in its harbour. Es Castell was founded by the British as Georgetown. What became of Menorca's registers under British rule is not established here.

eras.polity: France — captured in the Seven Years' War
eras.note: Sant Lluís was founded by the French as Saint-Louis. Britain regained the island in 1763 under the Treaty of Paris.
Franco-Spanish forces captured the island in 1782.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — recaptured; Britain ceded it back in 1783
eras.note: Britain ceded the island back to Spain at the Peace of Paris in 1783.
Britain captured the island again in 1798 and ceded it to Spain in the Treaty of Amiens in 1802.
The Balearics became a Spanish province in 1833. Parish registers are the record until civil registration in 1871.

Civil registration begins in 1871 under the law of 17 June 1870, though some municipalities have records from as early as 1837. The registers stay in each municipality's local archive; certified copies come from the Ministerio de Justicia or the local Juzgado de Paz / Oficina del Registro Civil.

eras.polity: Second Spanish Republic — Menorca loyal until February 1939
eras.note: Menorca stayed loyal to the Republic while the rest of the Balearics backed the Nationalists. There was no ground combat but Italian aircraft bombed it. The Nationalists took the island in February 1939, with the Royal Navy helping a peaceful transfer.
Under Franco's State.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Balearic Islands autonomous community
eras.note: The islands gained self-government under their first Statute of Autonomy in 1983.

regions.label: Ibiza and Formentera (the Pitiusas)
regions.sub: Sant Josep de sa Talaia, Sant Antoni de Portmany, Formentera

eras.polity: Conquest of Ibiza — the Kingdom of Majorca (from 1276)
eras.note: Before registers. Ibiza fell in 1235; the Kingdom of Majorca created in 1276 included Ibiza and Formentera. It passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1344 or 1349 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon — Kingdom of Majorca
eras.note: The Kingdom of Majorca remained separate, with its own viceroy, until the Nueva Planta decree of 1715.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Nueva Planta (Balearic province from 1833)
eras.note: The diocesan archive's index of sacramental books for Eivissa and Formentera says the books it does not list were destroyed in 1936; later ones are in the parishes. Listed baptism books begin in 1784 (Sant Antoni) and 1786 (Santa Agnès); for Sant Josep they begin only in 1888, and Formentera's Pilar parish lists baptisms from 1856 and deaths from 1784. Parish registers are the record until civil registration in 1871.

Civil registration begins in 1871 under the law of 17 June 1870, though some municipalities have records from as early as 1837. The registers stay in each municipality's local archive; certified copies come from the Ministerio de Justicia or the local Juzgado de Paz / Oficina del Registro Civil.
The Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931.

eras.polity: Francoist Spain — the Nationalist zone, after a Republican interlude
eras.note: Republican forces recaptured Ibiza early in the war and the Nationalists retook it in September 1936. Sources conflict on whether Formentera stayed loyal to the Republic. Under Franco's State.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Balearic Islands autonomous community
eras.note: The islands gained self-government under their first Statute of Autonomy in 1983.

regions.label: The Azores - nine islands
regions.sub: Ponta Delgada, Lagoa, Angra do Heroísmo, Horta, Flores, Corvo

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - the islands settled under captains-donatary
eras.note: Uninhabited until Portuguese settlement: a royal charter of 2 July 1439 authorised it and Santa Maria was settled that year under Gonçalo Velho, the first captain-donatary (the traditional landing date on Santa Maria is 15 August 1432, and early dates vary by source); São Miguel followed by about 1444, Terceira about 1450, Faial and Pico before 1466, Flores and Corvo were reached in 1452. Settlers came from mainland Portugal, with people from Flanders recorded on Terceira and enslaved Africans; the Diocese of Angra was created on 5 November 1534, and an earthquake and landslide buried most of Vila Franca do Campo on 21-22 October 1522, after which Ponta Delgada became the capital of São Miguel. The Azores government portal's online parish registers run from 1541.

eras.polity: Iberian Union - the Spanish Habsburg crown over Portugal's realm
eras.note: After the old king Henrique died on 31 January 1580 the succession passed to Philip II; São Miguel's councils pledged loyalty to him on 31 January 1581, but Terceira backed António, Prior of Crato, and beat a Spanish force at the Battle of Salga on 25 July 1581. A Franco-Portuguese fleet was defeated off São Miguel on 26 July 1582, and the Spanish landed on Terceira on 26 July 1583 and sacked Angra for three days. Portugal's own monarchy returned in 1640.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - the island captaincies
eras.note: The islands returned to a Portuguese king in 1640 and were still governed as separate captaincies; the captaincies were abolished by the Pombaline decree of 2 August 1766. Parish registers of this period sit in the three regional archives, not in one island series.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - Captaincy-General of the Azores, seat Angra
eras.note: On 2 August 1766 a single Captaincy-General of the Azores was created with its seat at Angra on Terceira (first holder D. Antão de Almada); an alvará of 23 February 1771 raised the archipelago to a province. The Constitution of 1822 introduced the term 'Ilhas Adjacentes' (adjacent islands), which stayed in use until 1976.

eras.polity: Liberal Regency of Angra - Terceira as the seat of the constitutional cause
eras.note: Liberals took the fortress at Angra on 12 July 1828 and the Junta Provisória proclaimed the Regency of Angra on 28 October 1828 (the 1829-1832 span often quoted is later than that source's start date); the Miguelists lost the Battle of Praia on 11 August 1829, the Marquis of Palmela reached Angra on 15 March 1830, and Liberal troops entered Ponta Delgada on 3 August 1831. D. Pedro reached Ponta Delgada on 22 February 1832 and the expedition left for Mindelo on 27 June 1832. Which side held an island at a given date mattered to who governed and taxed it, so check the date before reading an administrative record as 'Portuguese' in general.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - Province of the Azores, then three districts
eras.note: Decree no. 28 of 4 June 1832 abolished the Captaincy-General and created the Province of the Azores seated at Angra; decree no. 64 of 28 June 1833 split it in two, and the 1836 Administrative Code made three districts. The registers are kept by three regional archives: Ponta Delgada (Santa Maria and São Miguel), Angra do Heroísmo (Terceira, Graciosa, São Jorge) and Horta (Faial, Pico, Flores, Corvo); the Horta archive was created in 1965 and holds parish, notarial and civil material. Parish registers pass from the civil registry offices to the regional archives after 100 years, in five-year transfers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - districts with administrative autonomy
eras.note: The decree of 2 March 1895 gave administrative autonomy to districts that asked for it by a two-thirds majority: Ponta Delgada joined in 1895 and Angra in 1898, and the Horta district never asked. This was local administration inside the Kingdom, not the political autonomy of 1976.

The Republic was proclaimed on 5 October 1910 and the law separating Church and State was passed on 20 April 1911. The Civil Registry Code of 18 February 1911 made civil registration compulsory, and genealogy sources give 1 April 1911 as the date from which the civil register, not the parish book, was the legal record; pre-1911 parish books were ordered moved to the civil registry offices. The Azores portal's online parish registers end in 1911.

The Estado Novo ran from 11 April 1933 (constitution approved by referendum on 19 March 1933) to 25 April 1974. The Portuguese Wikipedia history of the Azores says nothing politically significant changed in the Azores under it before 1976; the First Azorean Congress met in 1938, and Britain was granted bases in the Azores in 1943 (Lajes on Terceira, 1944 agreement), which is where foreign service records can enter a family's story.

eras.polity: Portuguese Republic - the transition to autonomy
eras.note: The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 ended the Estado Novo. The Constitution of 2 April 1976 recognised political autonomy for the Azores, the provisional statute followed in Decree-Law 318-B/76 of 30 April 1976, and the first regional elections were held on 27 June 1976.

eras.polity: Portuguese Republic - Autonomous Region of the Azores
eras.note: The regional assembly's constituent session met in Horta on 21 July 1976 and the first Regional Government took office on 8 September 1976. Parish registers 1541-1911 and passport registers are searchable on the regional portal, with originals in the Ponta Delgada, Angra do Heroísmo and Horta archives; registers pass to those archives 100 years after the last entry.

regions.label: Madeira and Porto Santo
regions.sub: Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - Madeira and Porto Santo under donatary captaincies
eras.note: Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira reached Porto Santo in 1418 and, with Bartolomeu Perestrelo, Madeira in 1419; settlement began about 1420 or 1425 (sources differ; one gives c. 1425 under João I or Prince Henry). The archipelago was held by the Order of Christ, and the captaincies were Machico (1440, Tristão Vaz Teixeira), Porto Santo (1446, Bartolomeu Perestrelo) and Funchal (1450, João Gonçalves Zarco); Funchal became a vila in 1451. Before registers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - Madeira a crown possession
eras.note: A royal charter of 27 April 1497 made Madeira realenga (a crown possession), Funchal was raised to a city in 1508 and to a bishopric in 1514. FamilySearch's catalogue lists the Funchal Sé parish registers from 1538, the earliest date found for a Madeiran parish; the FamilySearch entry describes them as microfilms of manuscripts from the Funchal district archive.

eras.polity: Iberian Union - Madeira under Governors General
eras.note: During the union of the crowns the island was run by Governors General, the first being João Leitão. The news of the 1640 Restoration reached Madeira on 29 December 1640.
Madeira was part of the restored Portuguese kingdom.
The British first occupied Madeira 'amicably' on 23 July 1801 (Colonel William Henry Clinton as governor) and withdrew on 27 January 1802, after the Peace of Amiens.
Back under the Portuguese crown between the two British occupations.

British forces reoccupied Madeira in 1807. A Treaty of Restitution of 16 March 1808 returned the archipelago to civil administration, while other accounts keep the British on the island until 1814, so the end date is contested.

Madeira was an ordinary district of the Kingdom. The regional archive in Funchal publishes parish registers online, but how far back it does so differs from parish to parish; that is the online coverage, not the start of the books, so check its catalogue before concluding a register does not exist.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Portugal - autonomous district of Funchal
eras.note: The decree of 8 August 1901 established administrative autonomy in the Funchal district, using the powers set out in the decree of 2 March 1895. This was district self-administration inside the Kingdom, not the political autonomy of 1976.

The Republic was proclaimed on 5 October 1910. The Civil Registry Code of 18 February 1911 made civil registration compulsory; genealogy sources give 1 April 1911 as the date the civil register replaced the parish book as the legal record.
The Estado Novo ran from 11 April 1933 (constitution approved by referendum on 19 March 1933) to 25 April 1974.

eras.polity: Portuguese Republic - the transition to autonomy
eras.note: The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 ended the Estado Novo. The 1976 Constitution granted Madeira an autonomous administration with its own legislature.

eras.polity: Portuguese Republic - Autonomous Region of Madeira
eras.note: Political autonomy was granted in 1976, dated 1 July 1976 (Madeira Day) or 30 April 1976 depending on the source.

regions.label: New York — New Netherland, the Hudson Valley, Long Island and the north
regions.sub: New York City, Long Island, Albany, the Hudson Valley, Plattsburgh

eras.polity: New Netherland — Dutch West India Company, a province of the Dutch Republic from 1624
eras.note: The surviving New Netherland records are held by the New York State Archives in Albany, and translation of them has been published since 1974 by the New Netherland Project. Rensselaerswyck, the patroonship on the upper Hudson, began with land purchases in 1630 and covered most of what became Albany and Rensselaer counties.

eras.polity: Province of New York — the Duke of York's proprietary
eras.note: English forces took New Amsterdam in 1664 (dated 27 August or September 1664 depending on the source) and the province was named for its proprietor, the Duke of York. The Treaty of Breda of 23 July 1667 ended the war that had brought the capture.
The Dutch retook the colony on 9 August 1673, and the Treaty of Westminster of 19 February 1674 returned it to England.

eras.polity: Province of New York — proprietary, then royal from 1685
eras.note: The first colonial assembly was created in October 1683 and the province was divided into twelve counties on 1 November 1683; New York was part of the Dominion of New England from May 1688 to 1689. The governor's patent of 1685 made Rensselaerswyck a legal entity. The 1911 State Capitol fire destroyed much of the English colonial executive record held by the State Library, so surviving series are incomplete.

New York declared itself a state in 1776, adopted its first constitution in 1777 and ratified the US Constitution on 26 July 1788. A statewide registration law of 1847 failed through uneven compliance, so births, marriages and deaths before 1880-81 are found in church, cemetery and local records.

Statewide registration outside New York City began in 1880-81 (deaths from June 1880, births and marriages from 1881 depending on the source). New York City files its own birth and death certificates, and for Albany, Buffalo and Yonkers the state holds none before 1 January 1914. The state does hold births for Queens and Richmond for 1881-1897.

regions.label: Western and central New York — the Genesee Country and the Holland Purchase
regions.sub: Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, Binghamton, Ithaca

eras.polity: Province of New York — claim over Haudenosaunee lands
eras.note: Haudenosaunee lands lay within the Province of New York's claim. The Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783.

eras.polity: State of New York — Haudenosaunee lands, Massachusetts pre-emption
eras.note: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix of 1784 assured the Haudenosaunee that their lands stayed theirs unless they made new cessions. By the Treaty of Hartford of December 1786 Massachusetts held the right to buy Haudenosaunee land in the west, while New York kept sovereignty.

eras.polity: State of New York — Phelps and Gorham, Robert Morris, the Holland Land Company
eras.note: Massachusetts sold its pre-emption rights to Phelps and Gorham in April 1788, and the First Treaty of Buffalo Creek (8 July 1788) sold about 2,250,000 acres east of the Genesee River. The rights west of the river reverted to Massachusetts in March 1791, passed to Robert Morris, and were sold in 1792-93 in part to the Holland Land Company, a Dutch syndicate. The Preemption Line was resurveyed in 1792 about four miles west of the first survey, and New York accepted the corrected line on 24 March 1795.

eras.polity: State of New York — Holland Purchase
eras.note: The Treaty of Big Tree (September 1797) gave Morris title to the remaining Haudenosaunee lands west of the Genesee and created ten reservations. The Holland Land Company opened its Batavia office in 1802 and it operated until 1846; the company's main archive covers 1789 to 1869, and Cornell holds its records for Allegany, Cattaraugus, Chautauqua and Wyoming counties.
Birth, marriage and death registration outside New York City began in 1880-81; records for Albany, Buffalo and Yonkers before 1 January 1914 come from the local registrars, not the state.

regions.label: New Jersey — East and West Jersey
regions.sub: Newark, Jersey City, Trenton, Camden, Perth Amboy, Burlington

eras.polity: New Netherland (the Delaware shore also claimed as New Sweden, 1638-55)
eras.note: New Netherland included settlements in what became New Jersey, and its surviving records are at the New York State Archives in Albany. New Sweden lay along the lower Delaware River, in what is now Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, from 1638 until Dutch forces took Fort Christina on 15 September 1655.

eras.polity: Province of New Jersey — under the Duke of York's grant
eras.note: The surrender of Fort Amsterdam in September 1664 gave the English control of the region.
The Dutch Republic reasserted control for a brief period in 1673-74.

eras.polity: East Jersey and West Jersey — two proprietary provinces
eras.note: The province was divided into East and West Jersey in 1674, a split that lasted until 1702, and both were added to the Dominion of New England on 7 May 1688. The proprietors' records are now at the New Jersey State Archives in Trenton: the East Jersey board's moved from Perth Amboy after it dissolved in 1998, and the West Jersey Council of Burlington deposited its originals in December 2005. Probated deeds were filed with the provincial secretaries while land records stayed with the proprietors.

East and West Jersey were united as a royal colony on 17 April 1702, when both proprietary groups gave up their political rights; the proprietors kept their land records, so titles still trace to East or West Jersey surveys and deeds.

New Jersey adopted its first state constitution on 2 July 1776 and ratified the US Constitution on 18 December 1787. No 1790 census schedules for New Jersey are known to survive; the National Archives suggests they were probably destroyed in the British attack on Washington in the War of 1812.

Statewide registration of births, marriages and deaths began in May 1848; the State Archives holds originals from 1848 to about 1915-16 (the cutoff differs by source) and the Bureau of Vital Statistics holds later years. Municipalities kept duplicate registers from 1848, but many records from before 1910 have not survived.

regions.label: Pennsylvania — New Sweden and Penn's province
regions.sub: Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Erie, Harrisburg, Scranton, Lancaster

eras.polity: New Sweden — the lower Delaware (south-east Pennsylvania only)
eras.note: New Sweden lay along the lower Delaware River, beginning with the expedition that anchored on 29 March 1638 and ending when Dutch forces took Fort Christina on 15 September 1655. The American Philosophical Society holds a collection of New Sweden papers for 1640-1655, transcribed in 1820 from originals in Stockholm.

The Dutch annexed New Sweden to New Netherland in 1655, and the New York State Archives holds the surviving New Netherland records for the earliest settlements in what became New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware.

eras.polity: English — the Duke of York's colony
eras.note: England took the Delaware Valley from the Dutch in 1664; Pennsylvania did not exist as a colony until the grant to William Penn in 1681.

King Charles II granted the land to William Penn in 1681, and the Charter of Privileges of 1701 set up a provincial council and assembly. The province had long boundary conflicts with New York and Maryland. The baptism, marriage and burial registers of the Swedish congregation Gloria Dei in Philadelphia are digitised free by the Philadelphia Congregations Early Records Project.

Pennsylvania ratified the US Constitution on 12 December 1787. In the south-west, Virginia organised the ground as the District of West Augusta and created Yohogania, Monongalia and Ohio counties in 1776; the boundary with Pennsylvania was settled in 1780 (sources also give 1779 and 1785), and Pennsylvania formed Washington and Fayette counties from Westmoreland in 1781 and 1783. Yohogania County's court records for 1776-1780 are at the Washington County courthouse.

The state health department began issuing birth and death certificates on 1 January 1906, and the State Archives holds the early certificates. Before that, county Clerks of the Orphans' Court registered births and deaths in 1893-1906 with poor compliance (and in 1852-54); those registers are requested from the county courthouse.

regions.label: Delaware — New Sweden and the Lower Counties
regions.sub: Wilmington, New Castle, Dover, Lewes, Georgetown

eras.note: Fort Christina, built at the confluence of the Christina River and Brandywine Creek after the expedition of 29 March 1638, was the first permanent European settlement in Delaware; Dutch forces took it on 15 September 1655. The American Philosophical Society holds a collection of New Sweden papers for 1640-1655, transcribed in 1820 from originals in Stockholm.
The Dutch captured the Swedish colony in 1655 and annexed it to New Netherland.

eras.polity: English — the Duke of York's colony
eras.note: England took control in 1664, when Robert Carr took New Amstel and renamed it New Castle. The New Netherland Institute publishes the Delaware Papers for 1664-1682 from the New York State Archives.

eras.polity: The Lower Counties on the Delaware — leased to William Penn
eras.note: William Penn leased the three lower counties from the Duke of York in 1682, and they were governed as part of Pennsylvania until 1701, when they gained a separate legislature while sharing a governor with Pennsylvania until 1776.

The Delaware Assembly voted on 15 June 1776 to break ties with Great Britain and Pennsylvania, and Delaware was the first state to ratify the US Constitution, on 7 December 1787. No 1790 census schedules for Delaware are known to survive.

Birth and death registration began in 1861 under a law of 1860, with the Recorders of Deeds in the three counties; it was repealed in 1863 and not re-enacted until 1881. The Delaware Public Archives holds the 1861-1863 and 1881-1913 volumes, which are incomplete, and the state Bureau of Vital Statistics took over on 1 July 1913.

regions.label: Southern New England — Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island
regions.sub: Boston, Plymouth, Hartford, New Haven, Providence, Newport, Springfield

eras.note: Plymouth Colony was founded in 1620, with arrival at Cape Cod in November and settlement at Plymouth in December, and had no royal charter. The Massachusetts Bay Company's royal charter dates from 1629 (passing the great seals on 4 March 1628/9) and the Winthrop fleet sailed in 1630.

eras.polity: Separate colonies: Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut and Rhode Island
eras.note: Connecticut Colony was organised in 1636 (Fundamental Orders January 1639, royal charter 1662, with New Haven joining after 1664) and Rhode Island began at Providence in 1636 (Royal Charter 1663). Connecticut seized the Dutch post Fort Good Hope at Hartford in 1653. Plymouth remained a separate colony until 1691.

Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth were placed under the Dominion in 1686, Rhode Island and Connecticut were added, with Connecticut's laws replaced on 29 December 1687, and the Boston revolt overthrew it on 18 April 1689.

eras.polity: Province of Massachusetts Bay, Colony of Connecticut and Colony of Rhode Island
eras.note: Rhode Island resumed its charter government on 1 May 1689, and Connecticut readopted its earlier government. A new charter merged Plymouth into the Province of Massachusetts Bay, with Plymouth's legal end on 17 October 1691 and the province taking effect in 1692.

eras.polity: States of Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island
eras.note: Connecticut ratified the US Constitution on 9 January 1788, Massachusetts on 6 February 1788 and Rhode Island, the last of the thirteen, on 29 May 1790. Before statewide registration, births, marriages and deaths are in town clerks' books, published as Vital Records to 1850 for about 215 Massachusetts towns, as the Barbour Collection for Connecticut and in James N. Arnold's Vital Records of Rhode Island 1636-1850.

eras.polity: States of Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island
eras.note: Massachusetts began statewide collection of vital records in 1841, and the State Archives holds 1841-1930. Rhode Island began statewide registration in 1853 and Connecticut on 1 July 1897; for Connecticut between about 1850 and 1897 there is no statewide index, so the town of the event must be known.

regions.label: Northern New England — New Hampshire, Vermont and Maine
regions.sub: Portsmouth, Concord, Burlington, Montpelier, Portland, Bangor, Augusta

eras.polity: Proprietary grants to Mason (New Hampshire) and Gorges (Maine)
eras.note: Land grants of 1622 to John Mason and Ferdinando Gorges covered the coast between the Merrimack and Kennebec rivers; the area was split in 1629, when Mason named his part New Hampshire.
New Hampshire's settlements agreed in 1641 to be governed by the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and Maine's settlements were folded into it in the 1650s, beginning with York County.

eras.polity: Royal Province of New Hampshire; Maine under Massachusetts
eras.note: Charles II's charter of 1679 made New Hampshire a province, with government beginning in 1680, and both New Hampshire and Maine were in the Dominion of New England from 1686 to 1689. The Province of Massachusetts Bay, created in 1692, included all of present-day Maine.

eras.polity: Province of New Hampshire; Maine in the Province of Massachusetts Bay; the New Hampshire Grants
eras.note: New Hampshire's governor was shared with Massachusetts until 1741, when Benning Wentworth took office and the Massachusetts border was settled; Cumberland and Lincoln counties in Maine were created in 1760. In 1764 the Crown ruled in favour of New York over the New Hampshire Grants west of the Connecticut River (now Vermont), where land claims overlapped.

eras.polity: State of New Hampshire; District of Maine (Massachusetts); Vermont an independent republic
eras.note: New Hampshire became a state in January 1776 and ratified the US Constitution on 21 June 1788, and Massachusetts's constitution established the District of Maine on 25 October 1780. Vermont declared independence on 15 January 1777, took the name Vermont on 2 June 1777, and was admitted to the Union on 4 March 1791.

eras.polity: States of New Hampshire and Vermont; Maine part of Massachusetts
eras.note: Maine remained part of Massachusetts until it was admitted as the 23rd state on 15 March 1820; the 1790 census listed Maine on its own line, and Vermont was enumerated in 1791. The Maine State Archives directs searches for records before statehood to the Massachusetts Archives.

eras.polity: States of Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont
eras.note: Vermont town clerks recorded vital events from 1779, and an 1856 act created the state registry with annual lists from 1857. Maine's statewide registration begins in 1892, with earlier records at town level and the State Archives holding about eighty towns' pre-1892 records. New Hampshire's original records stay with the town clerks, and statewide recording is dated 1848, 1866, 1901 or 1905 depending on the source.

regions.label: Maryland - Chesapeake, Eastern Shore and the Potomac
regions.sub: Baltimore, Annapolis, St. Mary's City, Salisbury, Cumberland, Frederick

eras.polity: Province of Maryland - proprietary of the Calverts (Lords Baltimore)
eras.note: Chartered on 20 June 1632 to Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore; the first settlers landed on 25 March 1634 and St. Mary's City was the capital until 1695.
The proprietary charter was withdrawn after the Protestant Revolution of 1689 and the first Crown-appointed governor took office in 1692. The capital moved to Annapolis in 1695.

The Calvert proprietorship was restored in 1715. The Penn and Calvert grants overlapped on the northern boundary, which was disputed for about 80 years (hostilities from 1730, a ceasefire ordered in May 1738) and surveyed as the Mason-Dixon line in 1767.
Maryland declared independence in 1776, ratified the Articles of Confederation in 1781 and ratified the Constitution on 28 April 1788.

eras.polity: Maryland - Union state, Baltimore under federal martial law
eras.note: Maryland did not secede: the legislature voted 53 to 13 against secession on 29 April 1861. Union troops occupied Baltimore and declared martial law on 13 May 1861, and a new constitution abolishing slavery took effect on 1 November 1864.
Baltimore City recorded births and deaths from 1875 and the other counties from 1898; the Baltimore City vital records are held at the Maryland State Archives in Annapolis.

regions.label: Virginia - Tidewater, Piedmont, Valley and Southwest
regions.sub: Jamestown, Richmond, Williamsburg, Norfolk, Alexandria, Roanoke, Accomack

eras.note: Jamestown was founded on 14 May 1607 under the first charter of 10 April 1606; the charter of 23 May 1609 extended the colony 'from sea to sea', and the House of Burgesses first met on 30 July 1619.

A royal colony from 24 May 1624, when the Virginia Company's charter was revoked; the capital moved from Jamestown to Williamsburg in 1699. The Northern Neck Proprietary was demarcated by the Fairfax Line in 1746.
Virginia became a commonwealth on 4 July 1776 and ratified the Constitution on 25 June 1788.

The secession convention voted to secede on 17 April 1861 and voters ratified secession on 23 May 1861; Richmond became the Confederate capital in May 1861. The Library of Virginia lists many counties and cities, most in the east of the state, that lost early records to Civil War military activity, courthouse fires and natural disasters, and keeps surviving copies in its Lost Records Localities collection.

Virginia was restored to the Union on 26 January 1870. Statewide recording of births, marriages and deaths was required by an act of 11 April 1853; most localities did not record births and deaths from 1897 to 1911, and recording resumed in 1912.

regions.label: West Virginia - Virginia's counties west of the Blue Ridge
regions.sub: Wheeling, Charleston, Parkersburg, Martinsburg, Harpers Ferry, Morgantown

eras.note: Part of the Colony of Virginia, a royal colony from 24 May 1624.

eras.polity: Commonwealth of Virginia - the counties that became West Virginia
eras.note: Part of the Commonwealth of Virginia until 1863.

Virginia's secession convention voted to secede on 17 April 1861 and secession was ratified on 23 May 1861. Conventions at Wheeling in May and June 1861 declared its acts void, a Restored Government was organised with Francis H. Pierpont as governor on 20 June 1861, and voters approved statehood on 24 October 1861.

Admitted to the Union on 20 June 1863 as the 35th state; Berkeley and Jefferson counties voted in 1863 to join it. Virginia sued over those two counties in 1866, Congress recognised the transfer by joint resolution on 10 March 1866, and the Supreme Court ruled for West Virginia in 1870.

Counties first recorded births and deaths in 1853 under Virginia law; statewide registration began in 1917, county clerks hold the county registers, and the state death-certificate record books went to the West Virginia State Archives. The Supreme Court rejected Maryland's claim to land north of the South Branch Potomac in two decisions of 1910.

regions.label: The Carolinas - North and South Carolina
regions.sub: Charleston, Raleigh, Edenton, New Bern, Wilmington, Columbia, Greensboro

eras.polity: Province of Carolina - the Lords Proprietors
eras.note: Granted by charter of 24 March 1663 to eight Lords Proprietors and revised in 1665; the Albemarle settlement in the north dates from 1653 and Charles Town was founded about 1670.

eras.polity: North Carolina and South Carolina - proprietary provinces
eras.note: The division into North and South Carolina is dated 1712, though the partition was completed in 1710 and separation was not complete until 1729. The Yamasee War ravaged the South Carolina back-country in 1715-1717, and a rebellion against the proprietors in 1719 brought a Crown-appointed governor.

eras.polity: Royal colonies of North Carolina and South Carolina
eras.note: Both became royal colonies in 1729 when the proprietors sold to the Crown; North Carolina's royal status is dated 25 July 1729. North Carolina's capitals were Bath, Edenton, Brunswick and then New Bern.

eras.polity: States of North Carolina and South Carolina
eras.note: The colonies became states in 1776; North Carolina ratified the Constitution on 21 November 1789.

eras.polity: South Carolina and North Carolina - Confederate States
eras.note: South Carolina seceded on 20 December 1860 and North Carolina on 20 May 1861. Greensboro was the seat of the Confederate government until 5 May 1865.

eras.polity: States of North Carolina and South Carolina
eras.note: North Carolina was restored to the Union on 4 July 1868. North Carolina's statewide birth and death registration dates from an act of 10 March 1913 (the state vital records office holds births from October 1913); South Carolina's dates from 1915. Charleston city recorded deaths from 1821 and births from 1877.

regions.label: Georgia - the Trustees' colony, the Creek and Cherokee lands
regions.sub: Savannah, Augusta, Atlanta, Macon, Milledgeville, Columbus

eras.note: The charter was finalised on 9 June 1732 and Savannah was founded in February 1733. The charter banned slavery; it was permitted from 1749 and the ban was lifted by 1751.

The Trustees ceded the colony to the Crown in 1752 (the source article also gives 2 January 1755). Georgia was divided into eight parishes in 1758, and the Proclamation of 1763 extended its southern boundary to the St. Marys River.

Savannah was held by British forces from 29 December 1778 to 11 July 1782, and Georgia ratified the Constitution on 2 January 1788. Land taken from the Muscogee (Creek) and Cherokee nations was distributed by lottery from 1805 to 1833, the Cherokee were forcibly removed, and the lottery records are held by the Georgia Archives.
The secession ordinance is dated 19 January 1861 (a signed copy is dated 21 January). Atlanta was captured on 2 September 1864 and Union forces entered Savannah on 22 December 1864.

Georgia was readmitted to the Union on 15 July 1870. City registers began earlier than the state's: Atlanta births in 1896 and deaths in 1887, Savannah births in 1890. A 1919 law required statewide registration, with full compliance not until 1928.

regions.label: Kentucky - Fincastle and Kentucky counties of Virginia
regions.sub: Louisville, Frankfort, Lexington, Bowling Green, Paducah, Covington

eras.polity: Indian Reserve (Proclamation of 1763); Virginia's western claim
eras.note: Kentucky lay within the Indian Reserve created by the Royal Proclamation of 1763. The British purchased the Iroquois claim at Fort Stanwix in 1768, Fincastle County was formed in 1772, and the Transylvania Purchase at Sycamore Shoals dates from 1775.

eras.polity: Kentucky County, then Fayette, Jefferson and Lincoln counties, Virginia
eras.note: Virginia created Kentucky County by an act of 31 December 1776, effective early 1777. It was divided on 1 November 1780 into Fayette, Jefferson and Lincoln counties.
Admitted as the 15th state on 1 June 1792; Frankfort was named the capital in 1792.

eras.polity: Kentucky - neutral, then Union state; Confederate government at Bowling Green
eras.note: Neutrality was declared on 20 May 1861 and ended in September 1861. A Confederate convention at Russellville began on 18 November 1861 and named Bowling Green its capital; the Confederacy admitted Kentucky on 10 December 1861, and Bowling Green was abandoned on 11 February 1862, after which the state was largely under Union control.
Statewide birth and death registration was attempted from 1852 to 1862, then made mandatory from 1 January 1911, with general compliance by 1920.

regions.label: Tennessee - the Overmountain settlements, Franklin and the Southwest Territory
regions.sub: Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville, Chattanooga, Jonesborough, Clarksville

eras.polity: Indian Reserve (Proclamation of 1763); settlements within North Carolina's bounds
eras.note: The Proclamation of 1763 restricted settlement beyond the mountains, but settlers still moved west; the Watauga Association formed in 1772 within North Carolina's bounds.

eras.polity: State of North Carolina - western counties; the unrecognised State of Franklin
eras.note: Settlers organised the State of Franklin from 1784 to 1788; Congress did not recognise it, and the Franklinites agreed to rejoin North Carolina by early 1789.

eras.polity: Territory of the United States South of the River Ohio (Southwest Territory)
eras.note: North Carolina's legislature voted to cede the settlements on 22 December 1789, Congress accepted on 2 April 1790 and organised the territory on 26 May 1790. In 1790 it had the Washington District (Washington, Sullivan, Greene and Hawkins counties) and the Mero District (Davidson, Sumner and Tennessee counties); Knox and Jefferson counties were created in 1792.
Admitted as the 16th state on 1 June 1796.

Tennessee declared secession on 7 May 1861 and voters ratified it on 8 June 1861. Union forces took Nashville and Memphis in 1862 and the Confederates held East Tennessee, a Unionist area, until Union forces captured it in 1863; Andrew Johnson was appointed military governor in 1862.

Tennessee was readmitted to the Union on 24 July 1866. Statewide birth and death registration began in 1908, a 1914 law required registration and full compliance came in 1920; Memphis death records go back to 1 May 1848 and Nashville death records to July 1874.

regions.label: Florida
regions.sub: St. Augustine, Pensacola, Tallahassee, Jacksonville, Key West

eras.note: St. Augustine was founded in 1565. The Diocese of St. Augustine holds sacramental registers from 1594, the oldest Catholic parish records in the United States; the St. Augustine parish registers to 1821 have been digitised.

eras.polity: British East Florida and West Florida
eras.note: Spain gave Florida to Britain in 1763 in exchange for Havana, and Britain divided it into East Florida and West Florida. West Florida's capital was Pensacola, and Spain captured Pensacola in 1781.

The East Florida Papers (1784-1821), the archive of the Spanish government of East Florida, are in the Library of Congress, moved from Tallahassee in 1905; land-grant records stayed in Tallahassee. Spain moved West Florida's eastern boundary from the Apalachicola to the Suwannee River in 1785. The United States took possession on July 17, 1821 under the Adams-Onis Treaty signed in 1819.

Andrew Jackson governed as military commissioner in 1821 and Tallahassee became the capital. A territorial census in 1825 counted 13,554 people. The Second Seminole War ran from the end of 1835 to 1842.
Florida became the 27th state on March 3, 1845. The Third Seminole War ran 1855-1858.
Florida seceded on January 10, 1861. Union forces held Key West, Fort Jefferson and Fort Pickens at Pensacola throughout the war, and occupied Fernandina from March 1862; Tallahassee never fell.

Florida was readmitted to the Union on July 4, 1868. Statewide death registration is generally dated 1899 and birth registration 1917, with scattered earlier records (Key West from 1865, some deaths from 1877); sources differ on these start dates.

regions.label: Louisiana
regions.sub: New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Natchitoches, Lafayette, Shreveport

eras.note: Fort Maurepas (1699) was the first permanent settlement, Natchitoches dates from 1714, and New Orleans became the seat of civil and military authority in 1722. The French Superior Council records (1714-1769) are in the Louisiana Historical Center of the Louisiana State Museum; the Archdiocese of New Orleans' sacramental registers begin in 1718; the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence hold French colonial government papers.

eras.polity: Spanish Louisiana (west of the Mississippi and the Isle of Orleans)
eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain by treaty in 1762 (confirmed in 1763); the first Spanish governor arrived in 1766, settlers rebelled in 1768 and Spain enforced its rule in 1769. The Spanish Judiciary records (1769-1803) are in the Louisiana Historical Center and the New Orleans Notarial Archives hold French and Spanish notarial acts. The Florida Parishes east of the Mississippi were not part of Spanish Louisiana: they belonged to British West Florida from 1763 and Spain took Baton Rouge in 1779.

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase; Territory of Orleans (from October 1, 1804)
eras.note: France transferred Louisiana at the New Orleans Cabildo on November 30, 1803, and the United States took it on December 20, 1803. The Territory of Orleans was formed from the part of the Purchase south of the 33rd parallel; its 12 counties of 1805 were replaced in 1807 by 19 civil parishes. The Florida Parishes were annexed by the United States in 1810 and formally added in 1812.

In the Florida Parishes East Baton Rouge, Feliciana, St. Helena and St. Tammany were set up in 1810, Washington Parish in 1819, Feliciana was split into East and West Feliciana in 1824 and Livingston was cut from St. Helena in 1832, so an early record may sit in a parent parish.
Louisiana seceded on January 26, 1861. Union troops captured New Orleans on April 25, 1862.

Statewide birth and death registration is dated 1914, with parish-level records earlier; an Orleans Parish death index covers 1804-1967 at the Louisiana State Archives. Tangipahoa Parish was created in 1869 from parts of four older parishes.

regions.label: Alabama and Mississippi — Mobile, Natchez, the Gulf Coast
regions.sub: Mobile, Biloxi, Natchez, Vicksburg, Jackson, Montgomery, Huntsville

eras.note: Fort Louis on the Mobile River was founded in 1702 and rebuilt as Fort Conde in 1711, the start of present-day Mobile. French colonists also developed plantations in the Natchez district. Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence hold French colonial government papers.

The Treaty of Paris of February 10, 1763 gave Britain the land east of the Mississippi, which became West Florida with Pensacola as its capital; Mobile was in the colony and the Natchez District was organised within it in the 1770s.

eras.polity: Spanish West Florida (Natchez, Mobile); land north of 31 N claimed by the United States from 1783
eras.note: Spain took Natchez in 1779 and captured Mobile and Pensacola in the 1779-1781 campaign. The Spanish government archives of West Florida (1782-1816) are on NARA microfilm T1116, and the Natchez court and land records of 1767-1805 and the Natchez Chancery Court records from 1781 are published and microfilmed; the Mississippi Provincial Archives (Spanish Dominion) are at the Mississippi Department of Archives and History. Natchez passed to the United States in 1796 or 1798 depending on the source, while Mobile stayed Spanish until 1813.

The territory covered both states: Natchez was the first capital until 1802, Georgia's claim was ceded in 1802 and added in 1804, and the Mobile District of West Florida was annexed in 1812 and occupied in 1813. The Creek War of 1813-1814 ended with the Treaty of Fort Jackson on August 9, 1814.

eras.polity: Mississippi (state from December 10, 1817) and Alabama (Territory 1817-1819, state December 14, 1819)
eras.note: Alabama Territory was split from Mississippi Territory in 1817 and Alabama was admitted on December 14, 1819. The Choctaw ceded land at Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830 (removal 1831-1836), the Chickasaw at Pontotoc Creek in 1832 (removal mostly 1837-1838) and the Creek at Cusseta in 1832 (removal 1834-1837).

eras.polity: Confederate States of Mississippi and Alabama
eras.note: Mississippi seceded on January 9, 1861 and Alabama on January 11, 1861. Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, and Union occupation of Mississippi was partial: Natchez was occupied in 1863 and parts of the north earlier.

Alabama was readmitted in 1868 and Mississippi on February 23, 1870. Statewide birth and death registration began January 1, 1908 in Alabama and November 1912 in Mississippi (full compliance about 1921); earlier records are county-level, and a few Alabama counties kept registers from the mid-1880s.

regions.label: Arkansas
regions.sub: Arkansas Post, Little Rock, Fort Smith, Helena, Pine Bluff

eras.note: Henri de Tonti founded Arkansas Post in 1686, the first lasting European settlement in the state. The post was attacked by the Chickasaw in 1749.

France ceded the region to Spain in 1762 and Spain administered it from the late 1760s or 1771 depending on the source; the post moved to Red Bluff in 1779 and Fort Carlos III was built in 1781. Spain returned the region to France in 1800.

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase: District of Louisiana (1804), Louisiana Territory (1805), Missouri Territory (1812)
eras.note: The United States acquired the area in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Territory of Orleans was limited to ground south of the 33rd parallel, so Arkansas fell in the District of Louisiana and then, from 1812, in Missouri Territory, whose capital was St. Louis, until 1819.

eras.polity: Arkansas Territory (act of March 2, 1819, effective July 4, 1819)
eras.note: The territory was cut from the part of Missouri Territory south of 36 30 N and at first included present-day Oklahoma south of that line; its western parts were removed in 1824 and 1828. Arkansas Post was the capital to 1821 and Little Rock after; the 1820 census reported seven counties and the 1830 census 23.
Arkansas was admitted as a state on June 15, 1836. The Quapaw had been moved out of Arkansas to a reservation in northeast Oklahoma by 1833.
Arkansas seceded on May 6, 1861. Union forces took Fort Hindman at Arkansas Post in January 1863 and captured Little Rock in 1863, so Confederate control was partial from 1863.

Arkansas was readmitted on June 22, 1868. Statewide birth and death registration began on February 1, 1914; earlier events are in city, county and church records, and the state holds some Little Rock and Fort Smith deaths from 1881.

regions.label: Missouri
regions.sub: St. Louis, Ste. Genevieve, St. Charles, Kansas City, New Madrid

eras.note: The Illinois Country was attached to the province of Louisiana by royal order in 1717. Ste. Genevieve was founded around 1750 and St. Louis in 1764.

France ceded the land west of the Mississippi to Spain in 1763; Spain took control in 1763 or 1767 depending on the source, and the transfer to the United States was marked at St. Louis in March 1804. The civil records of the St. Louis area under French and Spanish rule are known as the St. Louis Archives, held at the Missouri Historical Society; French and Spanish land grant papers are at the Missouri State Archives.

eras.polity: District of Louisiana (1804), Louisiana Territory (1805), Missouri Territory (June 4, 1812)
eras.note: The Louisiana Territory was renamed Missouri Territory on June 4, 1812; the first five counties were organised on October 1, 1812. In 1819 the land south of 36 30 N, except the Bootheel, became Arkansas Territory; the 1820 census reported 15 counties.
Missouri entered the Union on August 10, 1821, and the capital moved to Jefferson City in 1826. The Platte Purchase of 1836-1837 added the northwest corner to the state.

eras.polity: Missouri (Union state; Confederate government in exile)
eras.note: Missouri did not secede. The Confederacy admitted it on November 28, 1861, but the exiled Confederate government controlled no part of the state. General Order No. 11 of 1863 cleared residents from rural Jackson, Cass, Bates and Vernon counties.

A voluntary birth registration law of 1863 let county recorders record births, and county clerks registered births and deaths from 1883 to 1893, after which registration lapsed until 1910; the Missouri State Archives hold the 1883-1893 microfilm. Statewide registration is dated 1910 or 1911 depending on the source.

regions.label: Ohio
regions.sub: Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati, Marietta, Chillicothe, Toledo

eras.note: Britain gained the region from France in the Treaty of Paris of 1763, and the Quebec Act of 1774 annexed it to the Province of Quebec. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 ceded it to the United States.

eras.polity: United States - land claimed by Virginia and Connecticut until their cessions
eras.note: Virginia ceded its western claims in 1784 but reserved the Virginia Military District, about 4.2 million acres between the Little Miami and Scioto rivers, to pay its Revolutionary War veterans in land. Connecticut ceded its western claims in 1786 but kept the Western Reserve strip in the northeast, which it sold to the Connecticut Land Company in 1795 or 1796.

Created by the Northwest Ordinance of 13 July 1787; the government was established at Marietta on 15 July 1788, with later capitals at Cincinnati (1790-1799) and Chillicothe (1799-1803). Connecticut ceded jurisdiction over the Western Reserve in April 1800. Virginia Military District land was surveyed by metes and bounds, not the rectangular survey used elsewhere, so claims are irregular and often overlap.

Ohio was admitted as a state on 1 March 1803. Virginia issued Military District grants until statehood; Congress extended the deadline for surveying and patenting claims several times, last on 3 March 1855, and on 18 February 1871 the unsurveyed, unsold remainder was ceded to Ohio. The Toledo Strip on the Michigan line was disputed in the Toledo War of 1835.

eras.polity: Ohio - county probate courts record births and deaths
eras.note: From 1867 each county's probate court recorded births and deaths as one-line entries in ledger books; an earlier law of 1856-57 was generally disregarded. There is no statewide index before 20 December 1908, so the county of the event must be known.

Statewide registration began on 20 December 1908. The Ohio History Connection holds death certificates from then (the end of its holdings is given as 1963 or 1970 depending on the source), and the Ohio Department of Health holds birth certificates from that date.

regions.label: Indiana
regions.sub: Indianapolis, Vincennes, Fort Wayne, Evansville, Corydon

eras.note: Vincennes, on the Wabash, was an older French settlement and trading post; Americans under George Rogers Clark captured it from the British in the Revolutionary War. Britain had gained the region from France in 1763, and the Quebec Act of 1774 annexed it to the Province of Quebec.
The Treaty of Greenville of 1795 ended the Northwest Indian War, and the native nations ceded southeastern Indiana and about two-thirds of present Ohio.

Created by an act signed 7 May 1800, in effect 4 July 1800, with Vincennes as capital until the seat moved to Corydon in 1813. Michigan Territory was split off on 30 June 1805 and Illinois Territory on 1 March 1809, so Indiana Territory's jurisdiction before those dates covered Michigan and Illinois ground as well.
Indiana was admitted on 11 December 1816 as the nineteenth state.

eras.polity: Indiana - county health offices record births and deaths
eras.note: Births and deaths from 1882 to 1906 are held mainly at the county level; the State Archives directs enquiries to the county health office where the event happened.
Statewide birth registration is dated October 1907; statewide death registration is dated 1899 or 1900 depending on the source.

regions.label: Illinois
regions.sub: Chicago, Springfield, Kaskaskia, Cahokia, Peoria, Rock Island, East St. Louis

eras.polity: New France - the Illinois Country, a French district of Canada
eras.note: The Illinois Country became a French district in 1675, when Marquette founded a Jesuit mission at the Grand Village of the Illinois. La Salle built Fort St. Louis on Starved Rock in 1682; settlers abandoned it in 1691.

eras.polity: French Louisiana - Upper Louisiana, the Illinois Country
eras.note: In 1717 the region passed from Canada to Louisiana. The first Fort de Chartres was built in 1718-1720, a second in 1725 and a stone fort completed about 1760.

eras.polity: Britain - east bank of the Mississippi
eras.note: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave the east bank to Britain and the west bank to Spain; the British took Fort de Chartres in 1765. St. Louis, founded in 1764 on the Spanish west bank, became capital of Upper Louisiana.

George Rogers Clark took the east bank for Virginia in 1778, and Virginia created Illinois County with Kaskaskia as its seat. The county was abolished and Virginia ceded its claims to the United States between 1782 and 1784 depending on the step.

eras.polity: Northwest Territory, then Indiana Territory from 1800
eras.note: Illinois ground was in the Northwest Territory from 1787 and in Indiana Territory from 1800 until Illinois Territory was created on 1 March 1809. Records of the 1800-1809 years belong to Indiana Territory, whose capital was Vincennes.
Illinois Territory existed from 1809 until statehood in 1818. In 1818 remnants of the territory were added to Michigan Territory.
Illinois became a state in 1818.

eras.polity: Illinois - county records of births and deaths
eras.note: Counties generally began recording births and deaths around 1877 (Will County, for example, from December 1877), with a few earlier records, and coverage varies by county.

A 1915 statute set up the first effective statewide registration, which began in 1916; not every county took part until 1922. The Illinois State Archives publishes a statewide death index for 1916-1950 and an ongoing pre-1916 death index, and copies of pre-1916 county records may come from the Illinois Regional Archives Depository where it holds that county.

regions.label: Michigan
regions.sub: Detroit, Lansing, Grand Rapids, Sault Ste. Marie, Marquette, Houghton

eras.polity: New France - Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit
eras.note: Cadillac's expedition founded Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit on 24 July 1701.

eras.polity: Britain - Detroit and the Great Lakes posts
eras.note: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 ceded Detroit to Britain and the 1783 treaty ceded it to the United States, but British forces stayed until they evacuated on 11 July 1796.

eras.polity: Northwest Territory, then Indiana Territory from 1800
eras.note: Michigan ground was in the Northwest Territory and from 1800 in Indiana Territory, until Michigan Territory was created by an act of 11 January 1805, effective 30 June 1805.

Detroit was the capital, and the great fire of 1805 destroyed nearly all of its colonial buildings. The British held Detroit from its capture in August 1812 until September 1813. The territory's boundaries moved: remnants of Illinois Territory were added in 1818, land east of the Missouri River in 1834, and Wisconsin Territory was split off on 3 July 1836.
Michigan was admitted on 26 January 1837, after the Toledo War of 1835, by giving up the Toledo Strip to Ohio and accepting the western Upper Peninsula.

eras.polity: Michigan - state registration law of 1867, unevenly enforced
eras.note: A law of 1867 required statewide registration of births and deaths, but it was not enforced early on. Pre-1897 death records and pre-1906 births are the most likely to be missing from state files.

A law of 1905 was much more effective, and full death-record compliance was generally reached by 1915. The Archives of Michigan digitises certificates from 1897 on Michiganology; the state vital records office holds records from 1867.

regions.label: Wisconsin
regions.sub: Milwaukee, Madison, Green Bay, Prairie du Chien, Mineral Point, La Crosse

eras.polity: New France - Green Bay and Prairie du Chien
eras.note: Jean Nicolet landed at Green Bay in 1634, and Nicolas Perrot established Fort St. Nicholas at Prairie du Chien in 1685. The British took control of Green Bay in 1761 and of all Wisconsin in 1763.
Wisconsin was annexed to the Province of Quebec in 1774, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 gave it to the United States.

eras.polity: United States - Northwest Territory (1787), Indiana Territory (1800), then Michigan Territory
eras.note: The British won the Siege of Prairie du Chien in July 1814, and the Treaty of Ghent in 1815 reaffirmed American jurisdiction. The first federal land offices opened at Green Bay and Mineral Point in 1834.

Congress created the territory on 20 April 1836 and it was organised on 3 July 1836. It first covered Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and part of the Dakotas, until Iowa Territory was created in 1838; the capitals were Belmont (1836), Burlington (1837) and Madison (1838-1848), so Burlington, in present Iowa, held 1837 territorial records.

eras.polity: State of Wisconsin - county registers of deeds record births and deaths
eras.note: Wisconsin became the 30th state on 29 May 1848. Before 1852 births, marriages and deaths were reported to county clerks and after 1852 to the county register of deeds; the law was not strictly enforced until roughly 1880. The Wisconsin Historical Society holds a statewide index to pre-1907 records that has gaps.
Statewide registration began on 1 October 1907, and the State Vital Records Office holds births from that date. One county source gives 1 June 1907 as the date the law took effect.

regions.label: Minnesota
regions.sub: St. Paul, Minneapolis, Duluth, Mankato, Fort Snelling, Rochester

eras.note: French explorers and fur traders arrived in the 1650s and 1660s, and Daniel Greysolon, Sieur du Lhut, helped arrange a Dakota-Ojibwe peace in 1679.

eras.polity: Spanish Louisiana west of the Mississippi; east of the river to the United States in 1783
eras.note: Land east of the Mississippi went to the United States under the 1783 Treaty of Paris and was part of the Northwest Territory from 1787. The western part passed from France to Spain in 1762, back to France in 1800 and to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase (west) and Northwest Territory lands (east): successive territories
eras.note: The western part moved through the District of Louisiana (1804), Louisiana Territory and Missouri Territory (1812), and Iowa Territory from 1838; the eastern part through Michigan and Wisconsin territories. Fort Snelling was begun in 1819.

Created on 3 March 1849 with St. Paul as capital, it also covered the eastern parts of present North and South Dakota. The 1850 census counted 6,077 people in nine counties, and Dakota treaties of 1851 opened much of the land to settlement. Statehood is dated 11 May 1858, a date some pages give as 24 May.
In the Dakota War of 1862, fighting broke out in the Minnesota River valley, and 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato on 26 December 1862; many other Dakota were confined and later exiled.

Statewide birth registration is dated 1900 and numbered death certificates 1908; deaths of 1900-1907 were recorded without certificate numbers. The Minnesota Historical Society holds death certificates and a birth index (births 1900-1934, with selected earlier records); certified copies come from the Minnesota Department of Health.

regions.label: North and South Dakota
regions.sub: Fargo, Bismarck, Yankton, Sioux Falls, Rapid City, Deadwood

eras.polity: Louisiana - Spanish from 1762, French again from 1800
eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762 and Spain returned it to France in 1800; the United States bought it in 1803. Large portions of both Dakotas lay in the Purchase.

Eastern Dakota ground was in Wisconsin Territory (1836), Iowa Territory (1838) and Minnesota Territory (1849); Nebraska Territory (1854) took ground west of the Missouri. Land left over when Minnesota became a state in 1858 was unorganised until Dakota Territory.

Created on 2 March 1861 from Nebraska Territory and unorganised land, it first included much of Montana and Wyoming; Idaho Territory took part in 1863 and Wyoming Territory in 1868. The capital was Yankton (1861-1883), then Bismarck. The Fort Laramie Treaty was signed in 1868 and gold was discovered in the Black Hills in 1874.

eras.polity: North Dakota and South Dakota - states
eras.note: An omnibus act signed on 22 February 1889 divided the territory, and North Dakota and South Dakota were admitted on 2 November 1889.
South Dakota's vital records law took effect in July 1905, with full compliance around 1932. North Dakota's statewide death registration is dated 1907 or 1908 depending on the source.

regions.label: Iowa
regions.sub: Des Moines, Davenport, Dubuque, Burlington, Iowa City, Sioux City

eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1762, and the Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave the west bank of the Mississippi to Spain; St. Louis, founded in 1764, became capital of Upper Louisiana. Spain returned Louisiana to France in 1800 and formally transferred it on 30 November 1803.
The ground was in Louisiana, Missouri, Michigan and Wisconsin territories before 1838. It was closed to white settlers until the 1830s, after the Black Hawk War.

Created in July 1838 and covering about 194,000 square miles including present Minnesota and parts of the Dakotas, with the capital at Burlington (1838-1841) and then Iowa City. The 1840 census counted 43,112 residents in 18 counties.
Iowa was admitted on 28 December 1846.
Statewide registration is dated 1 July 1880 for births or 1891 for deaths depending on the source, and compliance improved markedly after 1921.

regions.label: Nebraska
regions.sub: Omaha, Lincoln, Nebraska City, Grand Island, North Platte, Scottsbluff

eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762, Spain returned it to France in 1800, and the United States bought it in 1803.

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase lands - Missouri Territory, then unorganised
eras.note: Part of Missouri Territory from 1812, the area was unorganised federal land from 1821 to 1854. Fur-trading posts such as Fontenelle's Post and Fort Atkinson (founded 1819) preceded organised settlement.

Created by the Kansas-Nebraska Act on 30 May 1854 with Omaha as capital, it ran from 40 degrees to 49 degrees north. Colorado Territory (28 February 1861), Dakota Territory (2 March 1861) and Idaho Territory (3 March 1863) took parts of it.
Nebraska became a state on 1 March 1867; President Andrew Johnson's veto of the admission bill was overridden.
Statewide death registration is dated late 1904 and birth registration 1905 depending on the source; full compliance took several more years.

regions.label: Kansas
regions.sub: Topeka, Wichita, Kansas City, Lawrence, Leavenworth, Lecompton

eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762, Spain returned it to France in 1800, and the United States bought it in 1803.

eras.polity: Louisiana Purchase lands - Missouri Territory, then unorganised
eras.note: The area was part of Missouri Territory and then unorganised land.

Created by the Kansas-Nebraska Act on 30 May 1854, it ran from the Missouri line to the Rocky Mountains, so its western part became Colorado Territory in 1861. The capital moved among Pawnee, Fort Leavenworth, Lecompton and, de facto, Lawrence, and the territory had two rival legislatures and two constitutions.
Kansas was admitted as a free state on 29 January 1861 under the Wyandotte Constitution.
Statewide death recording is dated 1 July 1911 in one source and 1908 in another.

regions.label: Oklahoma - Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory
regions.sub: Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Tahlequah, Muskogee, Guthrie, Fort Gibson

eras.note: France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762, Spain returned it to France in 1800, and the United States bought it in 1803; Oklahoma is among the states the Purchase covered wholly or in part.

The ground was in Missouri Territory from 1812; the southern part of that territory became the Territory of Arkansaw in 1819, and the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819, finalised on ratification in 1821, moved the southwestern boundary.

eras.polity: Indian Territory - Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek and Seminole nations
eras.note: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 brought the Five Civilized Tribes, along with Plains and Great Lakes nations, to Indian Territory. Congress never organised it as a territory, and the nations governed themselves under treaties.

eras.polity: Confederate alliances with the Indian nations
eras.note: Confederate officers made treaties with the Five Civilized Tribes in June and July 1861, and Confederate forces took the US Army forts in the area. The Union recaptured the forts after Pea Ridge (March 1862) and essentially secured the territory after Honey Springs on 17 July 1863; the exact extent of Confederate-held ground is not fixed by the sources.

The Reconstruction treaties of 1866 required land concessions, emancipation of enslaved people and full tribal membership for freedmen. The Unassigned Lands were opened to settlement in the land run of 1889.

The Organic Act of 2 May 1890 combined the western half of Indian Territory with No Man's Land as Oklahoma Territory, with Guthrie as capital; land runs followed in 1890, 1891 and 1893, and Greer County passed from Texas in 1896. In Indian Territory the Dawes Commission was authorised in 1893 and the Curtis Act of 1898 ordered a new roll; the Dawes final rolls closed in March 1907 and list citizens by blood, by marriage and Freedmen.

Oklahoma became a state on 16 November 1907 by joining the two territories. Statewide birth and death registration began in October 1908; the state vital-records office holds no death records from before 1908 and only limited delayed birth records, while the Oklahoma Historical Society holds some earlier birth and death material tied to land allotments and tribal records.

regions.label: Texas — Spanish, Mexican, Republic and State
regions.sub: San Antonio, Nacogdoches, Austin, Houston, El Paso, Galveston

eras.polity: Spanish Texas — province of New Spain
eras.note: The first Spanish mission in East Texas dates from 1690, and San Antonio began in 1718 as a mission and presidio. The Bexar Archives (1717-1836) are held at the Briscoe Center, University of Texas at Austin, with part in the Bexar County Archives in San Antonio; the Nacogdoches Archives (dated 1729 or 1731 to 1836 depending on the source) are at the Texas State Library and Archives in Austin.

eras.polity: Mexican Texas — from 1824 the state of Coahuila y Tejas
eras.note: Under the 1824 constitution Texas was joined with Coahuila as the state of Coahuila y Tejas, and land was granted through empresarios under the colonization law (about 3,420 grant applications from immigrants and naturalised citizens). The Texas General Land Office holds land-grant records dating to the 18th century. The Law of April 6, 1830 prohibited further immigration by U.S. citizens.

Independence was declared on March 2, 1836. Statehood is dated December 29, 1845, but the Republic's government transferred power on February 19, 1846. Texas claimed the Rio Grande as its southern boundary while Mexico held to the Nueces; the State Library has a guide to pre-Republic and Republic records (1820-1845).

Texas entered the Union as the 28th state. In the Compromise of 1850 it gave up its claims to land now in Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Wyoming in return for $10,000,000 in federal bonds.

The Ordinance of Secession was adopted on February 1, 1861, approved by referendum on February 23, and took effect March 2, 1861 (the date Texas joined the Confederacy is given as March 2 or March 23 depending on the source). The last battle of the war, at Palmito Ranch, was fought on May 12, 1865, and Union troops took possession at Galveston on June 19, 1865.

Texas was readmitted to the Union on March 30, 1870. Statewide registration of births and deaths began in 1903 and of marriages in 1966; the State Library holds indexes, not the certificates, and county clerks hold property and local records.

regions.label: New Mexico and Arizona — Nuevo México to the Gadsden Purchase
regions.sub: Santa Fe, Albuquerque, Las Cruces, Tucson, Phoenix, Prescott

eras.polity: Spanish New Mexico — Santa Fe de Nuevo México
eras.note: Oñate founded the colony on July 12, 1598 and Santa Fe was founded in 1610. The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove the Spanish out for about 12 years until the reoccupation of 1692. The Spanish Archives of New Mexico (1621-1821) are held by the New Mexico State Records Center and Archives in Santa Fe.

eras.polity: Mexico — Territory of Santa Fe de Nuevo México
eras.note: New Mexico became a territory of Mexico in 1821. The Mexican Archives of New Mexico (1821-1846) are in the same State Records Center and Archives in Santa Fe. U.S. forces under Kearny occupied the province in 1846 and Mexico ceded it in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848.

New Mexico Territory was organised on September 9, 1850. Land south of the Gila River and west of the Rio Grande, including southern Arizona and the Mesilla Valley area disputed since 1848, came with the Gadsden Purchase (treaty signed December 30, 1853). In 1861-62 the Confederate Territory of Arizona was proclaimed for the part of the territory south of the 34th parallel; Union control returned after Glorieta Pass in May 1862.

eras.polity: New Mexico Territory and Arizona Territory
eras.note: The Arizona Organic Act of February 24, 1863 split the western part of New Mexico Territory off as Arizona Territory. In 1867 Arizona Territory's northwestern corner, west of the Colorado River, was transferred to Nevada.

eras.polity: United States — State of New Mexico and State of Arizona
eras.note: New Mexico was admitted on January 6, 1912 and Arizona on February 14, 1912. Statewide birth and death registration began in Arizona in 1909 and in New Mexico in 1920, though some New Mexico records exist from 1889.

regions.label: California — Spanish, Mexican and American
regions.sub: San Diego, Los Angeles, Monterey, San Francisco, Sacramento

eras.polity: Spanish Las Californias — mission and presidio frontier
eras.note: The first Alta California mission and presidio were founded at San Diego in 1769. The Santa Barbara Mission-Archive Library holds copies of the sacramental registers of the California missions; the Santa Barbara Presidio kept registers separate from the mission's.
Las Californias was split in 1804 and Alta California became a separate province. The 1819 Adams-Onís Treaty set its northern limit at 42 degrees north.

Mexico gained independence on August 24, 1821 and Alta California became a Mexican territory in April 1822; the missions were secularised from 1833.
